study.title: Ezekiel 6 - Judgment against idolatry and hope for a remnant
study.overview: Ezekiel prophesies against the mountains of Israel, that is, against the land marked by idolatry. The chapter announces complete destruction of the places of false worship, death scattered among the people and desolation of the land. At the same time, he preserves a hope: God will leave a remnant who will remember the Lord in exile, will recognize his guilt and hate the sin he has done. The ultimate purpose of judgment is that the people know that the Lord is indeed God, and that his word against unfaithfulness does not fail.

outline.title: Sentence against the mountains and idolatrous altars
outline.explanation: The prophet must turn his face to the mountains of Israel and announce that God will bring the sword against the high places, destroying altars, idols and images of the sun. The corpses of the worshipers will fall before the idols themselves, showing that idolatry does not protect anyone and that false worship will be profane by judgment.

outline.title: The remnant in exile and repentance
outline.explanation: Even after the devastation, God will preserve some fugitives among the nations. In captivity, they will remember the Lord, they will recognize that their hearts were unfaithful and will feel repulsed of themselves because of their abominations. Thus, exile will not only be punishment; it will also be an opportunity to awaken to the seriousness of the broken covenant.

outline.title: Prophetic mourning and total desolation of the earth
outline.explanation: Ezekiel must express with gestures the grief in the face of the disaster that comes: sword, famine and pestilence will reach the guilty. Where there was incense to idols, there shall be slain; and the land shall be made more desolate than the wilderness of Diblah, that all may know that the LORD has spoken with truth, and has fulfilled its wrath.

study.context: The chapter deals with Israel/Juda in his land and his religious infidelity. The notes highlight that the mountains of Israel were the political heart of the land and also the scene of many pagan shrines, the so-called high. The judgment announced reaches both the places of worship and the people who attended them. The notes also relate the remnant to exile among the nations, showing that the dispersion does not nullify the covenant of God, but reveals both his righteousness and his faithfulness.
study.theology: The central theme is the holiness of God before idolatry. The chapter teaches that religious sin is not a peripheral thing: it contaminates the earth, the altars and the life of the people. Judgment comes in a concrete, historical and comprehensive way, to show that the Lord is the only God and that his word against rebellion is serious. At the same time, grace appears in the remnant: God preserves some to lead them to repentance, so that divine discipline has not only punitive character, but also corrective and restorative. The proper answer to judgment is to remember the Lord, to recognize his own unfaithfulness and to abandon idols.

scholarViews.insight: The scope of judgment extends from Jerusalem to the mountains of Israel, which were the political center and were contaminated by pagan sanctuaries; the sentence falls on the land marked by idolatry.
God leaves a remnant, not by merit of them, but by mercy; this rest is preserved so that the people may recognize their unfaithfulness and the seriousness of judgment.
The mention of the mountains indicates the main scenarios of idolatry, and the prophet speaks of Judah, not of the northern tribes already brought into captivity.

questions: What, in practice, is responsible today with the honor due to the Lord in our hearts, time and trust?
How can God's discipline expose the seriousness of sin without failing to point to mercy?
Has our repentance included only sadness or real repulsion for the idols we follow?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to abandon every form of idolatry, not just visible images, but all that receives from our lives the trust, fear or worship that belongs to God. Confess concrete sins, ask the Lord for a broken heart and examine whether his faith produces obedient remembrance of the Lord, and not just religious language. If you go through discipline, loss, or exposition of sins, ask if God is using it to lead you to sincere repentance and an exclusive devotion.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided differ somewhat in the identification of Dibla/Diblateim and its possible relationship with Ribla; therefore, the reference of Ezekiel 6:14 was kept only at the contrast level with a known desert, without safely affirming the exact location. There is also not enough base in the notes to determine more historical details than what was explicitly said about the mountains of Israel, exile and the high idolaters.
